\chapter{Verbs That Break in the Middle --- the Stem Changers}
\label{ch:stem-changes}
\hlchaptermodality{69}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can express singular wanting and ability, compare the learned e-to-ie and o-to-ue changes, and say our with a known singular noun.}

Complete ES-C11-practice, the canonical closing checkpoint, and demonstrate singular querer and poder, the learned vowel-change contrast, and nuestro or nuestra before a known singular noun.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[querer]{querer — wanting with one familiar vowel change}

\label{lesson:ES-C11-querer}



\begin{quote}
You already say \textbf{tienes} and \textbf{tiene}, where the middle \textbf{e} opens into \textbf{ie}. Today, reuse that visible change in one useful verb and keep the same three-person frame you already own.
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item diphthong-ie — begin \textbf{quiero} with one smooth \emph{kye-} syllable.
  \item r-tap — end the infinitive \textbf{querer} with one light tap.
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{querer} means “to want.” With a person as its object, it can also express love, but wanting is the meaning used in this lesson.

It descends from Latin \textbf{quaerere}, “to seek or ask.” English keeps the same searching idea in \textbf{query}, \textbf{quest}, \textbf{inquire}, and \textbf{require}. Wanting something begins as seeking it.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: only the three singular forms}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{person} & \textbf{present of \textbf{querer}} \\
\midrule
yo & \textbf{quiero} \\
tú & \textbf{quieres} \\
él / ella / usted & \textbf{quiere} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Say the small set as \textbf{quiero · quieres · quiere}. The \textbf{e $\to$ ie} that you saw in \textbf{tienes, tiene} is visible again. The plural persons are deliberately left for a later step.

Place one known infinitive after the form of \textbf{querer}:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{Quiero hablar.} — “I want to speak.”
  \item \textbf{Quieres comer.} — “You want to eat.”
  \item \textbf{Quiere vivir.} — “He, she, or formal you wants to live.”
\end{itemize}

The second verb stays in its known infinitive form.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item “querer — quiero, quieres, quiere”
  \item “Quiero hablar”
  \item “quaerere — query — querer”
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{querer} mean? (“To want.”) Give the three learned forms. (\emph{Quiero, quieres, quiere.}) Which Latin verb and English cousin help explain it? (\emph{Quaerere}, “seek”; \emph{query} or \emph{quest}.) Next: add the other singular vowel change with \textbf{poder}.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[poder]{poder — ability with the o $\to$ ue change}

\label{lesson:ES-C11-poder}



\begin{quote}
\textbf{Quiero hablar} says what you want to do. Now change the first verb to say what you are able to do. The second verb will remain a known infinitive.
\end{quote}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item diphthong-ue — \textbf{puedo} begins \emph{pwe-} with one smooth glide.
  \item r-tap — end \textbf{poder} with one light tap.
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{poder} means “to be able”; in a sentence it often translates as “can.” It descends through Latin \textbf{potere} from \textbf{posse}, “to be able.” English \textbf{power}, \textbf{potent}, \textbf{potential}, and \textbf{possible} belong to the same family. Ability is the power to do something.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the three singular forms}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{person} & \textbf{present of \textbf{poder}} \\
\midrule
yo & \textbf{puedo} \\
tú & \textbf{puedes} \\
él / ella / usted & \textbf{puede} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Say \textbf{puedo · puedes · puede}. In these three learned forms, the stem \textbf{o} opens into \textbf{ue}. Plural persons wait.

Follow the form of \textbf{poder} with one unchanged infinitive:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{Puedo hablar.} — “I can speak.”
  \item \textbf{Puedes comer.} — “You can eat.”
  \item \textbf{Puede vivir.} — “He, she, or formal you can live.”
\end{itemize}

Compare \textbf{Quiero hablar} with \textbf{Puedo hablar}: only the first verb changes the meaning from want to ability.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item “poder — puedo, puedes, puede”
  \item “Puedo hablar”
  \item “poder — power — possible”
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does \emph{poder} mean? (“To be able; can.”) Give the three learned forms. (\emph{Puedo, puedes, puede.}) What English word is its close cousin? (\emph{Power.}) Next: compare only the singular forms you have actually learned.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[e to ie and o to ue]{e $\to$ ie and o $\to$ ue — compare the singular forms}

\label{lesson:ES-C11-stem-changes}



\begin{quote}
You now own three small singular sets: \textbf{tengo, tienes, tiene}; \textbf{quiero, quieres, quiere}; and \textbf{puedo, puedes, puede}. Compare only those learned forms before extending the pattern later.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
On the road from Latin to Spanish, many short \textbf{e} and \textbf{o} vowels opened when stressed: \textbf{e $\to$ ie} and \textbf{o $\to$ ue}. That history helps explain why a verb's stem can look different across its forms.

It is a clue, not a machine that predicts every form. Learn each verb's small set, then use the shared history to organize what you remember.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: two changes, one learned frame}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{person} & \textbf{\textbf{tener / querer}, e $\to$ ie family} & \textbf{\textbf{poder}, o $\to$ ue} \\
\midrule
yo & \textbf{tengo / quiero} & \textbf{puedo} \\
tú & \textbf{tienes / quieres} & \textbf{puedes} \\
él / ella / usted & \textbf{tiene / quiere} & \textbf{puede} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

The comparison says exactly this:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{querer} shows \textbf{ie} in all three forms learned here.
  \item \textbf{poder} shows \textbf{ue} in all three forms learned here.
  \item \textbf{tener} reminds you that a common verb may combine more than one change: \textbf{tengo} has its known \textbf{g}, while \textbf{tienes} and \textbf{tiene} show \textbf{ie}.
\end{itemize}

No plural form and no new verb is part of today's generalization.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item “quiero, quieres, quiere”
  \item “puedo, puedes, puede”
  \item “stressed e and o often opened to ie and ue”
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which change appears in \emph{querer}? (\textbf{e $\to$ ie}.) In \emph{poder}? (\textbf{o $\to$ ue}.) Why is the history useful but not a complete prediction rule? (It organizes learned forms, but individual verbs can combine or resist changes.) Next: one possessive that agrees with a known noun's gender.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[nuestro, nuestra]{nuestro, nuestra — “our” with singular gender agreement}

\label{lesson:ES-C11-nuestro}



\begin{quote}
You put \textbf{mi, tu,} or \textbf{su} before the known noun \textbf{café}. Now add “our” and let it match one contrast you learned much earlier: masculine \textbf{día} beside feminine \textbf{noche}.
\end{quote}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{nuestro} and \textbf{nuestra} mean “our.” They descend from Latin \textbf{noster}, also “our.” \textbf{Paternoster} means “Our Father,” and English \textbf{nostrum} originally meant “our thing.”

The change from \emph{noster} to \textbf{nuestro} also displays the historical \textbf{o $\to$ ue} opening you just used to organize \textbf{poder}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: match singular gender}]
\noindent
\begin{tabularx}{\linewidth}{@{}>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X>{\raggedright\arraybackslash}X@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{known noun} & \textbf{“our” phrase} \\
\midrule
\textbf{el día}, masculine & \textbf{nuestro día} \\
\textbf{la noche}, feminine & \textbf{nuestra noche} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabularx}

Like \textbf{mi, tu,} and \textbf{su}, the new word goes before the noun. Unlike those earlier forms, it shows the noun's gender: \textbf{nuestro} before a masculine singular noun, \textbf{nuestra} before a feminine singular noun.

Only these two singular forms belong to this lesson. Plural agreement and the separate word for “your” to a group wait.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item “nuestro día”
  \item “nuestra noche”
  \item “noster — nuestro — Paternoster”
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Which form goes before masculine \emph{día}? (\emph{Nuestro.}) Before feminine \emph{noche}? (\emph{Nuestra.}) What Latin source explains the pair? (\emph{Noster}, “our.”) Next: retrieve the whole chapter without adding a form.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[Practice]{Practice — wanting, ability, and our known nouns}

\label{lesson:ES-C11-practice}



\begin{quote}
This checkpoint adds nothing. Retrieve two three-form verbs, compare their two vowel changes, and choose \textbf{nuestro} or \textbf{nuestra} before one known singular noun.
\end{quote}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: the complete small chapter frame}]
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item wanting: \textbf{quiero · quieres · quiere} plus a known infinitive.
  \item ability: \textbf{puedo · puedes · puede} plus a known infinitive.
  \item the contrast: \textbf{e $\to$ ie} in the learned \emph{querer} set; \textbf{o $\to$ ue} in the learned \emph{poder} set.
  \item singular “our”: \textbf{nuestro día · nuestra noche}.
\end{itemize}

Plural persons and plural possessive agreement remain deferred.
\end{grammarlens}

\begin{cousinweb}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{querer} continues Latin \emph{quaerere}, “seek,” the family of \textbf{query}.
  \item \textbf{poder} continues the Latin ability family behind \textbf{power} and \textbf{possible}.
  \item stressed Latin \textbf{e} and \textbf{o} often opened into Spanish \textbf{ie} and \textbf{ue}.
  \item \textbf{nuestro, nuestra} continue Latin \emph{noster}, “our.”
\end{itemize}
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item “quiero hablar; puedo hablar”
  \item “quieres comer; puedes comer”
  \item “nuestro día; nuestra noche”
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Give the two singular sets. (\emph{Quiero, quieres, quiere; puedo, puedes, puede.}) Which vowel contrast organizes them? (\textbf{e $\to$ ie} beside \textbf{o $\to$ ue}.) Say “our day” and “our night.” (\emph{Nuestro día; nuestra noche.}) The next chapter can now build from this closed singular frontier.
\end{tcolorbox}
